BREAKING: US housing starts fell -5.2% MoM in September, to an annualized rate of 1.22 million, the 2nd-lowest reading since May 2020.

This follows MoM declines of -4.9% and -5.9% in July and August.

Single-family housing starts dropped -4.6% MoM last month, to 859,000, the 2nd-lowest since April 2023.

At the same time, multifamily housing starts fell -7.2%, to 349,000, the 2nd-lowest since May 2025.

Higher mortgage rates and worsening affordability are heavily weighing on housing demand.

Furthermore, elevated housing inventories and falling homebuilder confidence are discouraging new construction.

The US housing market is frozen.

AI-related borrowing is skyrocketing.

US Dollar-denominated AI-related corporate bond issuance is up to $419 billion so far in 2026, the highest annual figure on record.

This represents a +90% YoY increase from full-year 2025 and a +437% increase from full-year 2024.

Year-to-date, Alphabet, $GOOGL, Amazon, $AMZN, Meta, $META, Microsoft, $MSFT, and Oracle, $ORCL, have issued a combined $157 billion in corporate bonds, accounting for 37% of the total.

This is followed by investment-grade and high-yield data center and computing companies, which have raised $66 billion and $37 billion, respectively, and together account for ~25% of AI-related issuance.

Other AI-linked corporate bonds have represented $159 billion, or 38%.

The AI revolution is driving an unprecedented wave of corporate borrowing.

BREAKING: The 15 largest S&P 500 stocks now account for a record 46.7% of the index’s market value.

By comparison, during the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble, the 15 largest stocks accounted for 27.2% of the S&P 500.

The remaining 485 stocks represent just 53.3%  of the S&P 500’s market cap.

This comes as Nvidia, $NVDA, Apple, $AAPL, Alphabet, $GOOGL, and Microsoft, $MSFT, account for 7.5%, 7.1%, 5.9%, and 5.6%, respectively, or 26.1% combined.

This means just 4 stocks account for more than the next 11 combined.

Furthermore, the combined market cap of the 5 largest stocks now equals that of the bottom 434 stocks in the index, the largest gap on record.

Market concentration is at historic extremes.

The global debt crisis has never been worse.

Japan now has a gross government Debt-to-GDP ratio of 204.4%, the highest among any major world economy.

Italy follows at 138.4%, while the United States stands at 125.8%, which is only below the ~132.0% record set during the 2020 pandemic.

At the same time, France’s gross government Debt-to-GDP ratio is 118.4%, while Canada’s, China’s, and the UK’s are 110.7%, 106.9%, and 103.6%, respectively.

By comparison, Germany is the only major economy below 100.0%, at 64.6%.

The current average among advanced economies is 108.2%.

The world economy is drowning in debt.

The US affordability crisis is worsening:

Food prices have surged +34.5% since December 2019, now at their highest level on record.

Rent and grocery prices have risen +33.3% and +30.0%, respectively.

Furthermore, motor vehicle maintenance and repair prices have soared +55.2% over the same period.

Meanwhile, prices for services excluding rent, including medical care, transportation, education, communication, and recreation, have increased +29.2% since December 2019.

As a result, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) has risen +30.4%.

Basic necessities are becoming increasingly unaffordable in the US.

BREAKING: Hedge funds sold more global technology stocks in the 5 trading sessions ending October 15th than in any other 5-session period since 2016.

5-day sales were 2.6 standard deviations above the average over the last 12 months.

Over this period, the largest sales were recorded in the US technology sector, with semiconductor stocks accounting for 57% of US tech sales.

Meanwhile, in just 1 week, hedge funds reversed all cumulative purchases of AI stocks since the start of 2025, erasing nearly 2 years of accumulation in this group.

Despite the sales, hedge fund net exposure to global tech stocks remains higher than it has been 90% of the time over the last 5 years.

Hedge funds are reducing their exposure to tech at a record pace.
